title: the Sri Sukta
hook: a hymn heard when lamps are lit for Lakshmi opens with a portrait made of gold, silver and moonlight

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the stretch on Shakti as a philosophy with Vak, the goddess who speaks for herself: I move with the gods, I breathe out like the wind. Did you notice one bite of food happening through you? Day one thousand ninety.

Lamps along a windowsill. A doorway swept clean. A small plate of sweets, a few coins, a picture of a goddess seated on a lotus. In some homes and temples, when Lakshmi is worshipped, a hymn in old Vedic Sanskrit is chanted over all of it. It's called the Sri Sukta, the hymn to Sri. Yesterday the goddess spoke for herself. Today the voice turns around: a singer calls to her, and asks for her to come. The hymn goes on for some time, and this path will walk it slowly, one piece at a time. Today: what kind of hymn it is, and the first thing it sees when it looks at her.
screen: `LAMPS, A SWEPT DOOR, A LOTUS.` → `THE HYMN TO SRI.` → `NOT SUNG BY HER. SUNG TO HER.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Sukta means a hymn. Sri is the goddess, the one also called Lakshmi, and the word sri is heard as radiance, beauty and good fortune all at once. The hymn sounds Vedic: a singer, a fire, a request. Second, the first picture. The opening verse calls her golden in color, wearing garlands of gold and silver, shining like the moon, made of gold. That's the whole first look: not a story, not a battle, just light. Gold and silver are wealth, yes. But the moon is something else. Nobody can own moonlight, store it, or spend it. The hymn sets them side by side, and some readers hear the point there: the fortune the singer wants is bright the way gold is, and also cool and freely given, the way the moon is. Third, where this sits on the path. The last stretch was about Shakti as power: the power that lets Shiva stir, that holds up the gods, that breathes through every breath. In goddess worship, Lakshmi is that power seen as abundance. Not only money: food on the table, health, a peaceful house, a good name. Teachers read the hymn in more than one way. Some keep it plain, a household asking not to go without. Others hear it inwardly, as a prayer for the brightness of a good life. The hymn doesn't choose. Fourth, how it begins: with a request to someone else, the fire, to bring her. That's tomorrow. Today, just the portrait: golden, garlanded, moonlit.
screen: `SUKTA: A HYMN. SRI: RADIANCE, FORTUNE.` · `GOLDEN, GARLANDED, MOONLIT.` · `NOBODY CAN OWN MOONLIGHT.` · `SHAKTI, SEEN AS ABUNDANCE.` · then, large: `A PORTRAIT MADE OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: gold and moonlight. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one thing in your life that is like gold: something you worked for, earned, or keep safe. Hold it for a few breaths, with thanks. Then bring to mind one thing that's like moonlight: something good you never earned and can't own. A friend's laugh. A clear night. A stranger's kindness. Hold that too. Let both shine for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can name them before Lakshmi, or before God, in the words you already use. The bell holds the time.
The Sri Sukta. The hymn to Sri, called Lakshmi, which opens by seeing her golden, garlanded in gold and silver, and shining like the moon.
Your line: the Sri Sukta. Tonight, look for the moon, or any light you didn't make, and let it count as part of your fortune. Day one thousand ninety.

howItsDone: The Sri Sukta is chanted in Lakshmi worship, including in some homes and temples at Diwali, with lamps lit and offerings set before an image of the goddess.

original.note: Sanskrit: Sri Sukta, the hymn to Sri, the goddess also called Lakshmi.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn asking for money.
what it means: it opens with a portrait of light, gold beside moonlight, and readers hear both plain need and inner brightness in it.
what a scholar hears: verse 1, hiraṇyavarṇāṃ … suvarṇarajatasrajām, candrāṃ hiraṇmayīṃ lakṣmīm: gold, silver, moon, gold again.

notes: Sri Sukta 1 paraphrased: hiraṇyavarṇāṃ hariṇīṃ suvarṇarajatasrajām / candrāṃ hiraṇmayīṃ lakṣmīṃ jātavedo ma āvaha. 'hariṇī' (doe-like or yellowish) left out as uncertain. The request to Jatavedas is held back for day 1091; verse 2's anapagāminī is day 1092 (already written by another writer).
'Tradition keeps this hymn alongside the Rig Veda, among hymns added to it' refers to its place among the khila hymns; Keeper to confirm phrasing.
'the word sri itself carries radiance, beauty and good fortune' is a gloss of meaning, not an etymology; day 1093 treats Sri as a name more fully.
The gold/moon reading is attributed to 'some readers'.
howItsDone's Diwali and lamp details are general; Keeper to confirm.

Editor pass: cut the spoken claim that the hymn sits 'among hymns added to' the Rig Veda (a manuscript/collection claim the cited verse doesn't make; the khila placement stays only in the source ref); 'the word sri itself carries' softened to 'is heard as'; 'Lakshmi is that power seen as abundance' framed as goddess worship's view, not the narrator's.
